Q: Why is my cat peeing outside the litter box?
A: First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:

- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

passage.text:
Q: My dog eats grass. Is that normal?
A: Yes, it is very common, and most grass-eating dogs are not sick. Studies show fewer than 1 in 4 dogs vomit after eating grass. Dogs may eat grass for fiber, out of boredom or to get attention, or simply from instinct.

Things to watch:
- Grass sprayed with weed killers or pesticides can poison your dog. Keep him off treated lawns.
- Grass can carry worm eggs from other animals' poop. Ask your vet about regular deworming.
- If he seems bored or lonely, spend more time playing with him.

See your vet if he eats grass and then vomits often or seems to have stomach pain. That can point to a stomach or gut problem that needs checking.

question: How do I potty train my puppy?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: How do I potty train my puppy?
A: Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them if they finish there, and clean the mess well.

Q: My puppy bites and nips a lot. How do I stop it?
A: Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

Q: A bee stung my dog and his face is swelling up.
A: Swelling of the face, head or neck after a sting can become serious because it can block breathing. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the swelling is large or spreading, if he has any trouble breathing, or if he was stung inside the mouth or on the tongue.

While you get ready to go:
- If you can see the stinger, scrape it out sideways with a flat card. Don't squeeze it with tweezers.
- Hold a cold pack wrapped in a cloth on the swollen spot.
- On the way, watch his breathing closely.

Don't give him any human allergy medicine unless your vet tells you to. Even if the swelling seems mild, call your vet for advice.

question: How can I tell if my pet's problem is a real emergency or can wait?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: How can I tell if my pet's problem is a real emergency or can wait?
A: An emergency is any sudden, serious problem. If you're unsure, call your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. They can tell you whether to come in.

Go immediately if your pet:
- Has trouble breathing, breathes with the mouth open (cats), or has blue or very pale gums
- Is bleeding heavily
- Collapses, is unresponsive, or has a seizure
- Ate something poisonous
- Was hit by a vehicle or fell, even if they seem fine
- Is straining to pee with nothing coming out (especially male cats)
- Has a swollen belly and keeps retching (dogs)
- Suddenly acts very differently from normal

Save your vet's number and the nearest 24-hour clinic in your phone today, and know the route.

key: how do i safely move an injured dog or cat to the vet?
question: How do I safely move an injured dog or cat to the vet?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: How do I safely move an injured dog or cat to the vet?
A: Call your vet first, then leave as soon as you can. To move your pet safely:

- Protect yourself. Pain can make any pet bite or scratch. Covering the head and eyes with a towel can calm them.
- A cloth muzzle can help with dogs, but don't use one on flat-faced breeds or a dog with a chest injury, and never leave a muzzled dog alone.
- Keep the head, neck and spine as still as possible. Use a board, thick cardboard or a folded blanket as a stretcher.
- Put cats and small pets in a box or carrier with air holes.
- If something is stuck in the body, don't pull it out. Keep it from moving.
- Move slowly and avoid sudden jerks.

On the way, have one person drive while another watches the pet.

question: My cat got splashed with hot water/oil in the kitchen. How do I treat the burn?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: My cat got splashed with hot water/oil in the kitchen. How do I treat the burn?
A: Burns are often worse than they look, because fur hides the damage. Large or deep burns, burns on the face, and any chemical or electrical burn need a vet right away. To be safe, go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Before and on the way:
- Gently flush the area with cool water.
- Cover it loosely with a clean, non-stick dressing.
- Don't put creams or home remedies on it unless the vet says so.
- Wrap her in a towel and put her in a carrier to keep her calm.

If a chemical caused the burn, rinse with lots of water and bring the product label to the vet.

question: My cat is breathing with her mouth open and sitting hunched up. Is that normal?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: My cat is breathing with her mouth open and sitting hunched up. Is that normal?
A: No. In cats, open-mouth breathing is a sign of serious trouble and means she may not be getting enough oxygen. Fast or hard breathing, sitting or crouching in a stiff upright position, and bluish gums are also warning signs.

This is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

On the way:
- Keep her as calm and still as possible.
- Put her in a carrier or box with good air holes, and cover it lightly with a cloth to help her feel safe.
- Don't hold her tightly or press on her chest.
- Call the clinic ahead so the team can get ready for her.

passage.text:
Q: my cat is gagging and pawing at her mouth like something is stuck, help
A: She may be choking, so treat this as an emergency and call or go to a vet right away.

- Don't reach into her mouth with your fingers. A frightened cat can bite hard.
- If she can't breathe, give a few firm pats between the shoulder blades, or a few quick squeezes on both sides of the ribcage at the same time.
- Even if the object comes out, still have a vet check her.

On the way:
- Wrap her loosely in a towel and keep her calm.
- Have someone else drive so you can watch her breathing.
- If she stops breathing, call the clinic so they can guide you while you travel.

question: My dog got bitten by a snake in the yard. What should I do?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: My dog got bitten by a snake in the yard. What should I do?
A: Treat any snake bite as an emergency and go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even if the bite looks small. Some venoms, like cobra venom, cause little swelling but can affect breathing. Treatment works best when started early.

On the way:
- Keep your dog calm and limit his movement. Carry him if you can.
- Don't cut the bite, try to suck out the venom, or tie a tourniquet.
- Don't put ice, cold packs, heat or sprays on it.

Q: My dog got hit by a motorcycle but he's walking and seems okay. Does he still need a vet?
A: Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic as you leave so they're ready for him.

Q: my dog is having a seizure right now what do i do
A: Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

A: This sounds like heatstroke, which is an emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now.

Before you leave and on the way:
- Move him out of the sun into shade or an air-conditioned space.
- Wet his body with cool (not ice-cold) water or wet towels, especially the belly, and use a fan or the car aircon.
- Don't dunk him in a tub of cold water.
- Offer small sips of water only once he is alert and starting to cool.

Other heatstroke signs are hot skin, drooling, vomiting, and wobbly walking. Keep cooling him on the drive, and let the vet check him even if he seems to improve.

Q: My German Shepherd ate a big meal and then ran around. Now he's restless and drooling. Can bloat wait until morning?
A: No. Bloat (GDV), where the stomach fills with gas and can twist, is a life-threatening emergency. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour veterinary clinic now. Quick treatment greatly improves the chance of survival.

Signs to watch for:
- Restlessness and seeming uncomfortable
- Retching again and again with nothing coming up
- Lots of drooling
- A swollen, painful belly
- Fast breathing, pale gums, weakness

Large, deep-chested breeds like German Shepherds, Great Danes and Dobermans are at higher risk, especially when a big meal is followed by exercise.

On the way, keep him calm, don't give food or a lot of water, and call the clinic ahead so they can prepare.

Q: How often should I feed my puppy?
A: Puppies do best with small meals more often while young, then fewer meals as they grow. A common schedule:

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Q: How much water should my pet drink, and how do I spot dehydration?
A: Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: When should I spay or neuter my dog or cat?
A: The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer

Q: My dog or cat has bad breath. What causes it?
A: A healthy pet's breath should not smell bad. The most common cause is dental disease. Plaque and tartar build up on the teeth and inflame the gums, and the bacteria make the smell.

Bad breath can also point to other illness:
- Sweet or fruity smell: possible diabetes
- Urine-like smell: possible kidney disease
- Foul smell with vomiting, poor appetite or yellow gums: possible liver problems

What to do:
- Have your vet check bad breath that doesn't go away. A proper cleaning is done under anesthesia.
- Go sooner if you also see red or swollen gums, more drinking and peeing, weight loss, or poor appetite.
- At home, brush the teeth with pet toothpaste, ideally daily.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: How do I brush my dog's or cat's teeth?
A: Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Q: How often should I bathe my dog or cat?
A: Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

Q: How do I keep my cat cool during hot days?
A: Cats handle heat better than many dogs, but hot, humid days can still be dangerous.
- Keep fresh water in several places, and add wet food for extra fluids
- Give them a shaded, airy spot, and use a fan or air-con in the hottest hours
- Brush long-haired cats often to remove loose fur
- Never leave a cat in a parked car

Open-mouth panting, drooling, wobbliness or collapse can mean heatstroke. Move them somewhere cool and go to a vet now.

Q: Can I give my dog paracetamol for pain?
A: Please don't give human pain medicine to your dog without your vet's advice. Many common ones, including paracetamol and ibuprofen, can cause serious harm to dogs, and paracetamol is deadly to cats.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: Can cats get heartworm?
A: Yes. Cats get heartworm the same way dogs do, from mosquito bites, and indoor cats can be bitten too.

Signs can be mild or sudden:
- Coughing or asthma-like breathing attacks
- Vomiting, poor appetite, weight loss
- Trouble walking, fainting or seizures

Sometimes the first sign is sudden collapse. See a vet now if your cat has trouble breathing or collapses.

There is no approved medicine to cure heartworm in cats, and the dog treatment is not safe for them. That makes prevention the only real protection. Ask your vet for a heartworm preventive made for cats that suits your cat's weight and age.

Q: Can I use my dog's flea medicine on my cat?
A: No. Some flea and tick products that are safe for dogs are toxic to cats.

Stay safe:
- Only use a product labeled for cats, and check that it fits your cat's age and weight
- After treating your dog, keep your cat away from him until the product is dry
- Read the label every time
- Ask your vet before using any product on a kitten, a sick, old, pregnant or nursing pet

Go to a vet right away if your pet shows drooling, shaking or trembling, wobbly walking, seizures, vomiting or unusual tiredness after a flea product. Remove a flea collar at once if it causes a reaction. Bring the package with you.

passage.text:
Q: How often should adult dogs and cats be dewormed?
A: Parasite experts (CAPC) recommend year-round protection for adult pets. Many monthly preventives cover worms together with heartworm, fleas or ticks.

If your pet isn't on a year-round preventive:
- Deworm about four times a year
- Have a stool (fecal) test 2 to 4 times a year

Even on prevention, healthy adults should have their poop checked at least twice a year. Pets that hunt, roam, travel or mix with many animals may need it more often.

Ask your vet for a product that suits your pet's weight and age, and which worms are common where you live.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: What are the signs of tick fever in dogs?
A: "Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffness or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Q: I saw little white things like rice in my cat's poop. What is it?
A: Those are most likely tapeworm segments. They look like grains of rice or sesame seeds and may be stuck to the fur near the tail or in the poop. Cats usually get tapeworms by swallowing fleas while grooming or by eating mice or rats.

Other worm signs include:
- Vomiting or diarrhea
- A dull coat or potbelly, mostly in kittens
- Weight loss

See a vet today if you notice black, tarry poop, pale gums or weakness. Heavy hookworm or roundworm loads can cause serious blood loss, especially in kittens.

Bring a fresh stool sample to your vet. Treat for fleas too, or the tapeworms will come back.

Q: My cat has round bald patches. Is it ringworm?
A: It might be. Despite its name, ringworm is not a worm. It is a fungal skin infection. Signs include:
- Round patches of hair loss
- Broken or stubbly hair
- Scaly, crusty or red skin
- Dandruff or extra grooming

Ringworm spreads to people and other pets, and children are at higher risk. Its spores can stay in a home for many months.

What to do:
- See your vet, since flea allergy and other problems can look similar
- Keep the cat in one easy-to-clean room during treatment
- Wash hands after handling her
- Clean and disinfect the home well

Treatment often takes six weeks or more.

Q: My dog is losing hair and very itchy. Is it mange?
A: Mange is caused by tiny mites. Dogs get two main types:

Sarcoptic mange (scabies):
- Sudden, intense itching
- Bumps and crusts, often on the belly, chest, ears, elbows and legs
- Very contagious to other dogs, and can cause itchy skin in people

Demodectic mange (demodex):
- Bald, red, scaly patches, often with little itching
- Common in young dogs; mild cases may clear on their own
- The widespread form needs vet treatment

Your vet will usually do a skin scraping to check. Treat all pets that have contact with each other at the same time, and clean bedding and grooming tools. Follow your vet's treatment plan, which can take a while.

Q: What is heartworm and how does my dog get it?
A: Heartworms are long worms that live in the heart and lung blood vessels. Dogs get them from mosquito bites, which pass on tiny larvae that grow into adult worms over about 6 months. Indoor pets are at risk too, because mosquitoes come inside.

Many dogs show no signs at first. Later signs include:
- A mild cough that won't go away
- Tiring easily or not wanting to exercise
- Weight loss and poor appetite
- A swollen belly

Sudden trouble breathing, collapse or dark brown urine is an emergency. See a vet now.

Experts advise prevention every month of the year and a heartworm test every year. Ask your vet for a preventive that suits your dog's weight and age.

Q: My dog got into the trash and ate mouldy food. Now he's trembling.
A: Mouldy food, garbage and compost can contain mould toxins that cause tremors and seizures. Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Signs often start within 1 to 2 hours but can take several hours. They include vomiting, shaking, wobbliness, a fast heartbeat, overreacting to touch or noise, and seizures.

Before and on the way:
- Don't make him vomit, especially now that he's trembling, because he could inhale it or have a seizure.
- Keep him in a quiet, safe spot away from stairs and edges.
- Tell the vet what he got into, such as old bread, dairy or compost.

With hospital care, tremors usually settle in 1 to 3 days. Use bins with secure lids and keep compost fenced off.

- After a bite or scratch, wash the wound well and get post-exposure prophylaxis at an Animal Bite Treatment Center right away
- Vaccinate your dogs and cats every year

Q: At what age is my dog considered a senior?
A: There's no single age, because dogs age at different rates depending on breed and size. Vets often call a dog senior when it is in the last quarter of its expected lifespan. As a rough guide, many dogs reach this stage at around 7 to 8 years.

From that age:
- See the vet at least twice a year
- Ask about blood and urine tests every 6 to 12 months to catch problems early
- Have blood pressure and thyroid checked yearly

Watch for changes at home, like slowing down, drinking more, weight change or confusion, and tell your vet. Old age is not a disease. Many changes can be treated.

Q: How can I tell if my cat has arthritis?
A: Cats hide pain well, but arthritis is very common in older cats. Studies show more than 60% have it in at least one joint. Signs are often subtle:
- Not jumping up as high, or hesitating before jumping
- Avoiding stairs
- Trouble getting in and out of the litter box, or going outside it
- Grooming less, so the coat looks messy
- Sleeping more and being less active

Ways to help at home:
- Use a litter box with a low side
- Add steps or ramps to favorite spots
- Keep her at a healthy weight

Ask your vet for a check. Never give your cat human pain medicine unless your vet says so.

A: Arthritis (joint wear and pain) is common in older dogs. Look for:
- Stiffness, especially after resting
- Limping or a changed way of walking
- Trouble with stairs, jumping into the car or onto the sofa, or getting up
- Less interest in walks or play
- Thinner leg muscles
- Grumpiness or snapping when touched

What helps:
- Keep your dog at a healthy weight
- Gentle, regular exercise like leash walks
- Non-slip rugs and ramps at home

See your vet for a proper diagnosis and pain plan. Don't give any pain medicine, including human medicine, without your vet's advice.

A: Older dogs still need daily activity to keep their muscles, joints, weight and mind healthy. The type matters more than the amount:
- Choose gentle, low-impact exercise like shorter, more frequent leash walks or swimming
- Avoid lots of hard jumping and rough play
- Add brain games, new toys and simple training to keep the mind sharp

- Non-slip rugs or yoga mats on smooth floors
- Ramps for the bed, sofa or car
- Block stairs or pools if eyesight or hearing is poor

If your dog limps, stops often or is stiff after walks, he may be in pain. Ask your vet for a check and an exercise plan.

Q: My senior dog seems confused and paces at night. What's wrong?
A: This can be a sign of cognitive dysfunction, a condition like dementia in people. It affects about 14 to 22% of dogs over 8 years old. Signs include:
- Getting lost or stuck in corners at home
- Sleeping more in the day and restless at night
- Less interest in family members
- Toilet accidents in the house
- Pacing, anxiety or barking for no clear reason

Cats can get it too, and often meow more.

Pain, vision loss and other illnesses can cause similar changes, so see your vet for a full check. Treatment works best when started early. Gentle exercise, new toys and simple games can help keep your pet's mind active.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: Should I change my senior pet's food?
A: Maybe. Older dogs and cats have different needs:

Senior dogs:
- Usually need fewer calories, and gain weight easily
- May benefit from more fiber and good-quality protein to protect muscle

Senior cats:
- Often digest food less well, and may lose weight and muscle
- May need tasty, easy-to-digest, higher-protein food in smaller, more frequent meals

For both, aim for a healthy body shape, not too thin and not too heavy. Extra weight strains joints, while weight loss can be a sign of illness such as kidney disease.

Change foods slowly over several days. Ask your vet to check your pet's weight and muscle and suggest a diet that suits its health.

Q: Does my dog really need the lepto vaccine?
A: Leptospirosis is a serious bacterial disease that can also infect people. Dogs and rats can carry it and pass it out in their urine. The germs can survive for weeks to months in water and soil, and the risk goes up after floods and heavy rain.

The 2024 WSAVA guidelines say all dogs should be vaccinated where leptospirosis occurs and suitable vaccines are available.

In general:
- The first course is two doses given 2 to 4 weeks apart
- After that, a booster is usually needed every year

Keep your dog out of floodwater and puddles when you can. Your vet will tell you if lepto vaccine is right for your dog and when to give it.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: How often does my adult dog need booster shots?
A: It depends on the vaccine:
- Distemper, parvovirus and adenovirus: after the puppy series and an early booster (at about 6 months or 1 year old), modern vaccines protect for years. Global guidelines advise boosting no more often than every 3 years.
- Leptospirosis: protection is shorter, so it is usually given every year.
- Rabies: some vaccines last 1 year and some 3 years, but in the Philippines the rules of the Anti-Rabies Act (RA 9482) require a yearly anti-rabies shot.

Your vet will make a booster plan based on your dog's age, health, lifestyle and the products used.

Q: My pet seems sleepy after her shots. Normal or not?
A: Mild reactions are common and should be short-lived:
- Soreness or a small swelling where the shot was given
- Tiredness or less appetite
- Mild fever
- Vomiting once

Allergic reactions are less common but can be serious. Severe ones usually start within minutes to an hour, but other reactions can appear hours later. Go to a vet now if you see:
- Swelling of the face, lips or eyes
- Hives (raised bumps on the skin)
- Repeated vomiting or diarrhea
- Trouble breathing
- Weakness or collapse

Call your vet if mild signs do not improve or you are unsure. Always tell your vet about any past reaction before the next vaccine.

key: what does 5-in-1 or 6-in-1 vaccine mean?
question: What does 5-in-1 or 6-in-1 vaccine mean?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: What does 5-in-1 or 6-in-1 vaccine mean?
A: The number tells you how many diseases one shot protects against. Combining them means fewer injections.

Labels often use letters, for example:
- D = distemper
- A2 = adenovirus type 2 (protects against hepatitis)
- P = parvovirus
- P = parainfluenza
- L = leptospirosis

So "DA2PP" covers four diseases, and adding L gives "DA2LPP". Products differ in what they add, such as extra lepto strains or other germs, so the number alone doesn't tell you the exact mix.

For cats, the common combo is FVRCP: feline viral rhinotracheitis (herpesvirus), calicivirus and panleukopenia.

Ask your vet which diseases your pet's vaccine card covers.

key: what is parvo and why is it an emergency?
question: What is parvo and why is it an emergency?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: What is parvo and why is it an emergency?
A: Parvovirus is a very contagious virus that attacks a dog's gut. Puppies and unvaccinated dogs are most at risk. It spreads through infected poop and anything it touches, and it can survive in the environment for months or longer.

Signs usually start 5 to 7 days after exposure:
- Dullness, fever and not eating
- Then vomiting and diarrhea, often bloody

Dogs lose fluids fast and can go into shock. Some die within hours, but most dogs that get hospital care survive. See a vet now if your puppy has vomiting or bloody diarrhea. Call ahead so the clinic can protect other patients.

Keep sick dogs away from others. Ask your vet how to disinfect your home, because many cleaners don't kill parvo.

key: what vaccines does my dog need
question: what vaccines does my dog need

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: Which vaccines are core for dogs?
A: Core vaccines are the ones every dog should get, wherever it lives. For dogs these protect against:
- Distemper
- Parvovirus
- Adenovirus (infectious hepatitis)

Rabies vaccine is also core anywhere the disease is present or the law requires it.

Global guidelines now say leptospirosis vaccine should be given to all dogs in places where the disease occurs, so in those areas it is treated as core too.

Other vaccines, like kennel cough (Bordetella and parainfluenza), are "non-core". Your vet suggests them based on your dog's lifestyle, such as boarding or contact with many dogs. Ask your vet which vaccines suit your dog.

key: when does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
question: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: When does my puppy start his shots, and why so many?
A: Puppies usually get their first core vaccine at 6 to 8 weeks old. Shots are then repeated every 2 to 4 weeks until the puppy is at least 16 weeks old.

Why a series? Antibodies from the mother's milk protect a young puppy, but they also block vaccines from working. These antibodies fade at a different age in each puppy, so repeat shots make sure one of them "takes". The dose given at 16 weeks or later is the most important.

Global guidelines also advise another core dose at around 6 months old instead of waiting until 1 year, to catch puppies that did not respond earlier.

Your vet will set the exact schedule for your puppy.

Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Q: My cat isn't eating. How long is too long?
A: Don't wait it out. A cat that stops eating can develop a serious liver problem called hepatic lipidosis (fatty liver). It can be fatal if not treated quickly. Overweight cats are at higher risk.

What to do:
- If your cat hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours, take her to the vet now.
- Go right away if her gums, ears, skin or the whites of her eyes look yellow, or if she is very weak.
- Tell the vet when she last ate and if anything changed at home.

Most cats with fatty liver have another illness that caused the poor appetite, so the vet will look for that too. Fatty liver needs prompt treatment, so don't wait to see if she starts eating again.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

See your vet within 24 hours. The vet needs to look at the ear canal and eardrum and find the cause before choosing a treatment. Some ear medicines can cause hearing loss if the eardrum is torn, so don't use leftover or store-bought drops on your own.

Go now if he is in severe pain. Go today if the ear flap suddenly swells up. Left untreated, ear infections can damage the eardrum and cause lasting hearing loss.

Q: My dog or cat has diarrhea. When do I need a vet?
A: Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.

passage.text:
Q: My cat is sneezing and has runny eyes. Is it cat flu?
A: It may be an upper respiratory infection, often called cat flu. Viruses like feline herpesvirus and calicivirus are common causes, and they spread easily between cats. Signs include sneezing, runny eyes or nose, mouth sores, tiredness and poor appetite.

What helps:
- Gently wipe her nose clean. A blocked nose can stop her smelling food, so she may eat less.
- Make sure she keeps eating and drinking.

See your vet within 24 hours if the sneezing doesn't stop. Go now if she:
- Has trouble breathing, or her gums look bluish
- Hasn't eaten properly for 24 hours
- Is a kitten. Young cats are more likely to get seriously ill.

Vaccines can make these infections milder.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: My cat is vomiting. Is it just hairballs?
A: Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: My dog is vomiting. Can I treat him at home?
A: One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

key: my dog isn't eating. when should i worry?
question: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?

passage.label: FurFriends checked answer
passage.text:
Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

Q: My dog keeps shaking his head and scratching his ears. What's wrong?
A: This is a common sign of an ear infection. Other signs are red ears, a bad smell, dark or yellowish discharge, and pain when you touch the ear. Allergies are often behind it, and dogs with floppy or hairy ears get them more often.

Q: My dog isn't eating. When should I worry?
A: A dog that stops eating is often unwell, so take it seriously and involve your vet early.

What to check:
- Does he seem hungry but struggle to pick up, chew or swallow food? That points to pain in the mouth, teeth or jaw.
- Has anything changed lately, like a move, a new food or a new medicine?
- Are there other signs, like vomiting, diarrhea, pain or low energy?

When to go:
- Skipped meals but otherwise acting normal: see your vet today, within 24 hours.
- Go now if he hasn't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or if he is also vomiting, very weak or in a lot of pain.
- If he has diabetes and refuses even one meal, call your vet right away.

question: Bleeding that won't stop in my cat. Is this serious?

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Snake bite
passage.text:
Snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.
Signs: A sudden yelp, swelling, puncture marks; Bleeding that won't stop; Drooling, wide pupils, trembling; Weakness, wobbliness, trouble breathing, collapse
What to do now:
1. Keep yourself safe. Don't try to catch or kill the snake. Take a photo from a distance if it's easy.
2. Keep your pet calm and still, and carry them if you can.
3. Take off the collar if the bite is on the head or neck, because it may swell.
4. Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.
Don't: Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice. Waiting for signs to appear.
Go to a vet now.

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Stings & allergic reactions
passage.text:
Stings & allergic reactions. Bee, wasp, ant and centipede stings usually cause swelling that settles. A spreading reaction or trouble breathing is an emergency.
Signs: Mild: swelling and pain where they were stung, licking the spot; Go now: the face swells and keeps spreading, or hives all over the body; Go now: vomiting, diarrhea, pale gums, weakness or collapse; Go now: trouble breathing, a sting inside the mouth or throat, or many stings
What to do now:
1. Move away from the insects.
2. If you see a bee stinger, scrape it out sideways with a card. Don't squeeze it.
3. Hold a cold pack wrapped in cloth on the spot for 10 minutes.
4. Watch closely for the next 1–2 hours and call your vet for advice.
Don't: Giving human allergy or cold tablets without a vet's dose. Some contain decongestants that are toxic to pets.
Call your vet for advice.

key: blue or pale gums, collapse. my dog is like this right now, what should i do?
question: Blue or pale gums, collapse. My dog is like this right now, what should I do?

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Choking
passage.text:
Choking. Something stuck in the mouth or throat. If your pet is still breathing and coughing, go to the vet. Only step in if they can't breathe.
Signs: Pawing at the mouth, gagging or retching; Panic, struggling to breathe; Blue or pale gums; Collapse
What to do now:
1. Stay calm and hold them gently but firmly. A choking pet may bite.
2. Open the mouth and look. If you can see the object and get a grip on it, remove it carefully with fingers or tweezers.
3. If you can't remove it and they can't breathe: hold a cat or small dog with their back against your chest and give 5 firm thrusts inward and upward just below the ribs.
4. For a large dog, put your arms around the belly from behind, make a fist just below the ribs and push firmly up and forward 5 times. If they're lying down, push from behind the ribs toward the head.
5. Check the mouth again and repeat. If they collapse and stop breathing, start CPR.
6. Go to the vet even if the object comes out. The throat may be injured.
Don't: Sweeping your fingers blindly. It can push the object deeper. Pulling on string, thread or tinsel hanging from the mouth or bottom. It can cut the intestines.
Go to a vet now.

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Trouble breathing
passage.text:
Trouble breathing. Breathing problems can come from heart disease, asthma, injury or allergic reactions. They are always urgent.
Signs: Open-mouth breathing in a cat; Neck stretched out, elbows held out, belly heaving; More than 40 breaths a minute at rest; Blue, grey or pale gums; noisy breathing
What to do now:
1. Keep them calm and cool, and handle them as little as possible.
2. Loosen or remove a tight collar or harness.
3. Let them pick the position that's comfortable. Carry small pets in an open carrier.
4. Go to the vet now, with the car's air-con on.
Don't: Holding them tightly or covering their face. Offering food or water.
Go to a vet now.

question: Afterwards: confused, wobbly, briefly blind in my cat. Is this serious?

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Seizures
passage.text:
Seizures. Most seizures stop within 2 minutes. Keep your pet safe, time it, and call your vet.
Signs: Collapse, stiff or paddling legs; Jaw chomping, drooling, losing control of pee or poo; Not responding to you; Afterwards: confused, wobbly, briefly blind
What to do now:
1. Stay calm and note the time it starts.
2. Move furniture and objects away, keep them away from stairs and water, and put a towel under the head. Keep your hands away from the mouth.
3. Dim the lights and keep things quiet. Film it if you can, since it helps the vet.
4. Afterwards, keep them somewhere quiet and cool, and speak softly while they recover.
5. Call your vet after any first seizure. Go now if it lasts over 5 minutes, they have another one, they don't wake up between seizures, or they may have eaten a poison.
Don't: Putting fingers or anything else in their mouth. Pets can't swallow their tongue. Holding them down. Giving food, water or medicine until they're fully alert.
Go to a vet now.

key: doesn't respond when you call or touch them, no heartbeat on the left side of the chest, just behind the elbow. my dog is like this right now, what should i do?
question: Doesn't respond when you call or touch them, no heartbeat on the left side of the chest, just behind the elbow. My dog is like this right now, what should I do?

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: CPR
passage.text:
CPR. Only for a pet who is unconscious, not breathing and has no heartbeat. Get someone to drive to the vet while you work.
Signs: Doesn't respond when you call or touch them; No chest movement for 10 seconds; No heartbeat on the left side of the chest, just behind the elbow
What to do now:
1. Lay them on their right side on a firm surface. Put flat-chested breeds like Bulldogs on their back.
2. Cats and small dogs: wrap one hand around the chest just behind the elbows and squeeze. Larger dogs: stack both hands on the widest part of the chest. On their back: press on the breastbone.
3. Push hard and fast: a third to a half of the chest's width, 100–120 times a minute (the beat of "Stayin' Alive"). Let the chest come all the way back up.
4. After 30 compressions, close the mouth, straighten the neck and give 2 quick breaths into the nose, watching the chest rise.
5. Keep going 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Check for breathing and a heartbeat every 2 minutes, and keep going on the way to the vet.
Don't: CPR on a pet who is breathing or has a heartbeat. It can hurt them.
Go to a vet now.

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Burns & electric shock
passage.text:
Burns & electric shock. Chewed electric cords, hot water and chemicals are the usual causes. Electric shock can cause breathing problems hours later.
Signs: Red, blistered or raw skin; singed fur; Burns at the corners of the mouth after chewing a cord; Coughing or trouble breathing; Collapse
What to do now:
1. Electric shock: switch off the power or unplug before you touch them. If you can't, push them away with something dry and wooden, like a broom handle.
2. Check breathing, and start CPR if they aren't breathing and have no heartbeat.
3. Heat burns: run cool water over the area for 10 minutes, then cover with a clean, damp cloth.
4. Chemical burns: wear gloves and rinse with plenty of running water for 15–20 minutes. Stop them licking it.
5. Go to the vet, even if they seem fine.
Don't: Touching a pet that's still in contact with electricity. Ice, butter, oil or creams on burns. Popping blisters.
Go to a vet now.

question: My dog has thick drool, bright red or very pale gums. Help, what do I do?

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Heatstroke
passage.text:
Heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.
Signs: Heavy panting, or noisy breathing (any panting in a cat is a warning sign); Thick drool, bright red or very pale gums; Vomiting or diarrhea; Wobbly, weak or confused; collapse or seizures
What to do now:
1. Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
2. Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
3. Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
4. Keep cooling for 10–15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
5. If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 °C so they don't get too cold.
Don't: Ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling. Leaving a wet towel draped over them. It traps heat. Wet the coat and keep air moving instead. Waiting to see if they recover on their own.
Go to a vet now.

question: My dog has sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth. Help, what do I do?

passage.label: FurFriends first-aid guide: Toad poisoning
passage.text:
Toad poisoning. Cane toads, the large brown toads that come out after rain, release a poison when a dog or cat bites or licks them.
Signs: Sudden heavy drooling or foaming at the mouth; Pawing at the mouth, shaking the head; Bright red gums; Vomiting, wobbliness, a racing heartbeat, seizures
What to do now:
1. Rinse the mouth straight away. Point the head down and run a gentle stream of water across the gums and tongue from the side, so it flows out of the mouth. Keep going for 10 minutes.
2. Wipe the gums and tongue with a damp cloth to remove the sticky poison.
3. Go to the vet now, especially if there's anything more than drooling.
Don't: Spraying water down the throat. It can go into the lungs. Making them vomit.
Go to a vet now.
